planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in warm conditions or plant container-grown vines after last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Amazon vine tolerates salt spray better than its relative S. ciliatum, making it a good choice for exposed coastal gardens.

directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings and train on a trellis, fence, or arbor in full sun to part shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Amazon vine is a South American twining vine closely related to the more commonly grown orchid vine, Stigmaphyllon ciliatum, sharing the same clusters of fringed, butter-yellow, orchid-like flowers and samara-style winged seed pods. It is distinguished from its relative chiefly by greater salt tolerance, making it a better choice than S. ciliatum for exposed coastal Gulf Coast and South Florida gardens where salt spray limits other flowering vines. It climbs rapidly on a trellis, fence, or pergola and blooms over a long warm season. Protect from temperatures below 30F, since like other Stigmaphyllon species it is damaged or killed back by hard frost; established plants typically resprout after a mild zone 9 winter dieback.

common_name: Foxfibre Cotton (Sally Fox's Naturally Colored Organic Cotton)

planting.note: Direct sow 1/2 to 1 inch deep once soil has thoroughly warmed well past last frost, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; needs the same long, hot, frost-free season as any cotton.

directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the growing season is reliably warm, following standard upland cotton culture. Foxfibre is the trademarked line of naturally colored, organically grown upland cotton developed by California breeder Sally Fox beginning in the 1980s from a chance discovery of brown, pest-resistant cotton seed; through years of selection and crossing with long-staple and Pima lines, Fox produced the first naturally colored cotton fiber strong and long enough to be spun on modern commercial machinery. Foxfibre bolls open in shades of camel, tan, rust-brown, and soft sage green that need no dye, and the plants show useful natural pest resistance. Pick bolls promptly once open, since color and fiber quality fade with prolonged weather exposure, and rotate the planting site yearly to limit soil-borne disease buildup as with any cotton.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; this rare Chilean species is slower and lower-growing than the related Ugni molinae.

directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Ugni candollei is a rare, small evergreen shrub endemic to the coastal regions of central and southern Chile, growing in habitat similar to its better-known relative Ugni molinae (Chilean guava). It stays lower and denser than Chilean guava, typically reaching only 2 to 2.5 feet, with small white five-petaled flowers followed by edible, pink to light-orange berries, a paler color and slightly different flavor than the deep-red fruit of Ugni molinae. Grow it as a specimen or low hedge in mild, humid, acidic-soil gardens, and protect from hard freezes, since it has cold tolerance limits similar to Chilean guava.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in fertile, humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; propagate by softwood or semi-hardwood cuttings rather than seed to preserve the variegated leaf pattern.

directions: Plant container-grown specimens in fertile, humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, propagating by cuttings rather than seed to preserve the leaf variegation. Carnival is a brightly variegated clone of Clerodendrum trichotomum var. fargesii, the harlequin glorybower, with upright, bushy, deciduous growth bearing grey-green leaves broadly margined in creamy-white to pale yellow. In late summer it opens jasmine-scented, white to pink-tinged starry flowers set in showy red calyxes, followed in fall by glossy, porcelain-blue berries that persist as the red calyxes age to deep violet, creating a striking two-tone fruit display against the variegated foliage. It tolerates drought once established. As with the species, the foliage has an unpleasant odor when crushed; site it where the fall berry display can be enjoyed without brushing the leaves.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or grafted trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; David is an extremely cold-hardy Ussurian pear hybrid that needs a second hardy pear nearby for pollination.

directions: David is a cross between the classic European Bartlett pear and the extremely cold-hardy Ussurian pear (Pyrus ussuriensis), bred to survive prairie and northern winters where standard European pears fail outright, and reported to tolerate temperatures of -50F or colder once established. Like other Ussurian-type hybrids, the medium-to-small, round, golden fruit is powerfully astringent, especially if picked underripe, and is best used for cooking, hard cider, and perry blends rather than fresh eating unless left to fully ripen and soften. Plant with a second cold-hardy pear such as Ure or Rescue nearby for cross-pollination, and expect a vigorous, disease-resistant tree well suited to zone 2-3 gardens where fruit tree choices are otherwise limited.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Nova is self-fertile but fruit set and size improve with a second cold-hardy pear planted nearby.

directions: Nova was introduced by St. Lawrence Nurseries in northern New York, one of the oldest cold-climate fruit nurseries in North America; unlike the Manitoba- and Saskatchewan-bred Ussurian hybrids such as Ure, Rescue, and David, Nova's exact parentage was never formally documented, and it has long circulated in cold-climate nursery trade based on performance rather than pedigree. It is reliably hardy to zone 3 and has proven successful even in parts of Alaska, tolerating winters that eliminate most European pear cultivars. Nova stands out among cold-hardy pears for genuine fresh-eating quality, described by growers as flavorful whether picked slightly green or left to fully ripen, a comparatively rare trait among the often gritty, astringent Ussurian-derived hardy pears. It is also self-fertile, though fruit set and size improve with a second hardy pear planted nearby.

common_name: Frances Gaulter Bearded Iris (Ruffled Pink-and-Violet Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun; Frances Gaulter is a tall bearded iris registered by hybridizer Melba Hamblen and introduced by Mission Bell Gardens in the early 1980s, a cross of Sugarplum Fairy and Heavenly Harmony. It grows about 34 inches tall and blooms in late midseason, with pink standards over violet falls, both laced and ruffled at the edges, set off by a tangerine-red beard. Though less commonly grown today as a garden plant in its own right, it holds a lasting place in iris breeding history as a parent of Schreiner's Gardens' 1993 introduction Celebration Song, crossed with Lullaby of Spring. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor and flowering.

common_name: Lullaby of Spring Bearded Iris (Yellow-and-Lavender Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; hybridized and introduced by Schreiner's Gardens.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun; Lullaby of Spring is a tall bearded iris hybridized by Schreiner's Gardens and introduced in 1987, described in the nursery's introductory catalog as a milestone new color pattern. It grows about 38 inches tall with an early midseason bloom of pure lemon-yellow standards over soft, warm lavender falls, the large, rounded blossoms carrying a distinctive waxy-finished texture. Beyond its own garden merit, it holds a lasting place in iris breeding history as a parent of Schreiner's 1993 introduction Celebration Song, crossed with Frances Gaulter. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor and flowering.
